item.title: A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
item.description: Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian) is a city on the left bank of the Dnipro River, across from Kherson on the right bank. Only nine kilometers (about six miles) separate them in a straight line. People once crossed between them by bridge, but the bridge is now closed. The two cities are on opposite sides of the front: Ukraine controls Kherson, while Russia has controlled Oleshky since 2022. As in other cities near the front, life in Oleshky is difficult and dangerous. By September 2026, conditions had deteriorated so badly that people in both Ukraine and Russia were calling the situation critical. Those who remain are trying to survive without food, electricity, and adequate medical care. They cannot leave safely and often cannot even bury their loved ones. Here is what Meduza has been able to learn about conditions in the city.

Israel wants US-led force to disarm Lebanon's Hezbollah
item.description:
Fearing a security vacuum if UN peacekeepers leave southern Lebanon when their mandate expires December 31, the Lebanese government is desperately seeking an extension of the United Nations Interim Force (UNIFIL) or the creation of a European-led multinational force to take its place.

Israel, which has occupied dozens of villages south of the Litani River since its latest invasion of the country earlier this year can't wait for the Blue Helmets to leave. It has long lobbied against UNIFIL’s extension, deeming it ineffective in taming and disarming Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militia.

But Tel Aviv hasn't opposed an international force once UNIFIL leaves; it just doesn’t want one tied to the UN. Israel is lobbying for a U.S.-led force, while the Lebanese government prefers a European-led mission to aid the Lebanese army if UNIFIL’s mandate is not renewed or extended.

An even bigger question is how exactly any such force can subdue battle-hardened Hezbollah, the country’s most powerful armed force. The group has long enjoyed widespread support in the Shiite community, which makes up about a third of the country’s total population.

Days before the UN General Assembly meeting in New York this week, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun visited Paris where he met with French President Emmanuel Macron and Jordan's King Abdullah. They discussed the need for the continued presence of foreign troops and the importance of making that clear to President Donald Trump.

Israel occupied five key points in Southern Lebanon after Hezbollah joined the war between Israel and Hamas in 2023. Israel rained bombs on a region inhabited mostly by Shiite Lebanese and forced them to flee to other parts of the country. A ceasefire was inked first in November last year although Israel never fully stopped bombing. Clashes broke out again in March after U.S. and Iran assassinated Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei and Hezbollah attacked Israel, offering it an excuse it needed to keep the war going and a justification to hold the occupied territory.

The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) are ill-equipped to push back against the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in the south. Residents there fear that UNIFIL's withdrawal could leave them vulnerable to a prolonged or even permanent Israeli presence.

UNIFIL's exit would also mean losing a neutral party and "the world's eyes and ears" in a region where misunderstandings can quickly escalate into armed conflict. Roughly 7,500 troops from 46 countries have monitored airspace violations and land incursions, offering a vital de-escalation liaison since the 2006 Israeli-Hezbollah war.

Moreover, UNIFIL troops have served as a lifeline for people in Lebanese villages who refused to leave their homes after the Israelis arrived and established their “security zone.” For instance, UN troops navigate Israeli checkpoints to deliver humanitarian aid, medicine, and food convoys to the residents of a Christian town called Rmeich. Their departure could halt the delivery of supplies and sever the link between these villages and the rest of the country.

Considering the circumstances, an extension of six months to a year appears to be a reasonable ask.

But Israel is preoccupied with disarming Hezbollah and seemingly unconcerned about Lebanon’s internal political dynamics. It has long derided UNIFIL as ineffective and has been waiting for it to leave. It got its wish last year, when, under U.S. pressure, the UN Security Council extended UNIFIL's mandate only until the end of this year.

Since it was created in 1978 after the first Israeli invasion of Lebanon, UNIFIL has always been an irritant for Israel. It was reinforced after the 2006 war under UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which called for the area between the Blue Line — the de facto Israel-Lebanon border — and the Litani River to be completely demilitarized apart from deployments there by the LAF and UNIFIL.

Israel, which was supposed to withdraw its forces from the area as the LAF and UNIFIL deployed there insists that the peacekeepers never fully enforced the resolution, while UNIFIL argues it was never tasked with forcibly disarming Hezbollah.

This has been a source of major tension between Israel and the UN, and, by extension, with Lebanon. Now, Israel wants a force empowered to disarm Hezbollah, militarily if necessary, and prefers a U.S.-led mechanism to carry that out.

A problem with that plan, however, lies in Washington’s unwillingness to deploy its own troops. Europeans, on the other hand, are willing to provide troops, as they have in the past, but prefer to deploy them under a UN mandate. However, if Israel manages to convince Washington to keep the UN out – which Washington can do by virtue of its veto power on the Security Council – the Europeans will likely resort to a “coalition of the willing” model – mustering a group of countries willing to deploy troops and aid the LAF on a multilateral basis.

Several European countries have already established an Italian-led technical military support group to aid the LAF and enhance its capacity. The European Union (EU) has said that more than 10 countries are ready to contribute troops to a post-UNIFIL international force.

The UN itself has tabled three options with varying numbers of uniformed soldiers constituting the actual force who would also be accompanied by armed soldiers for force protection. It has also listed requirements for monitoring equipment such as radars, helicopters, and satellite imagery. The proposal calls for a deployment that ranges from 2000 to 5000 troops, depending on the plan.

Under the first option, UN troops could potentially conduct joint operations with the LAF even north of the Litani River, closer to Beirut. The second option proposes "some" joint operational activities with the LAF, only south of the Litani, although it also offers verification of any violations of UNSCR Resolution 1701 north of the river "on a limited basis." The third would have more limited means, and limited capacity to coordinate between the IDF and the LAF.

The key question, however, remains unanswered: What kind of joint operations are European nations willing to carry out alongside the LAF?

Israel does not trust the LAF’s willingness or ability to disarm Hezbollah and wants an international force capable of carrying out a door-to-door search and seizure of Hezbollah's weapons. That is a risky undertaking for any international forces, however.

EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas said the objective of such a force is to "strengthen the Lebanese armed forces and the ability of the Lebanese state to provide security across its territory." That presumably covers less dangerous tasks, such as training and providing key equipment.

There is no clarity on what an international post-UNIFIL force would eventually look like. But several plans could potentially merge: the U.S. could join a UN-led mission composed of European forces. Israel hopes that Washington will at least provide its state-of-the-art satellite surveillance systems to ensure Hezbollah’s adherence to UNSCR 1701. And it demands that any post-UNIFIL force operate with a much stronger mandate and more teeth than either the EU or the UN have so far proposed.

But the kind of force Israel wants – one that will go door to door to disarm Hezbollah – is a nightmare for the Lebanese government which is worried. A large number of Shiites in the country support Hezbollah. Any such force may have to confront Hezbollah’s supporters and that may lead to civilian casualties, even a civil war. Moreover, Shiites are a part of the LAF, a coercive disarmament could lead to mutiny.

And if Israel’s plan is to occupy southern Lebanon indefinitely, as some top Israeli officials have suggested, Tel Aviv risks strengthening Hezbollah and its calls for resistance, while weakening the state authorities. Improving ties with Beirut is Tel Aviv's best shot at achieving a mutually acceptable arrangement that ushers in a functioning peace.

Disarming Hezbollah is not solely a military endeavor; it will require a painstaking intra-Lebanese political process that eases concerns among the Shiites about their standing in a deeply sectarian society. Regional actors, such as Turkey and Saudi Arabia, will also want a say. And the elephant in the room will have to be addressed at some point. Iran will not just walk away and abandon Hezbollah, an ally, especially not when it appears to be winning the war started by the US and Israel.

NATO Can’t Count Its Way to Maritime Superiority
item.description:
Allied navies are still counting hulls. The contest at sea is now about who sees, decides, and acts first.

Earlier this month, Western officials disclosed that American, British, and Norwegian forces had tracked and confronted Russian deep-sea units near Svalbard this spring as they rehearsed a method for disabling undersea cables. The Russian vessels were stopped before they finished the sabotage and left the area. The confrontation matters less than how it was won. The Allies saw the activity in time to act.

That is the right lens for NATO's maritime future.

For four centuries, the sea hid things. Distance, weather, and the Earth's curvature made finding a fleet harder than fighting one. Navies were built accordingly. They concentrated their combat power on a small number of survivable platforms and used the ocean's opacity to arrive where the enemy was not.

That premise is failing.

Commercial satellite imagery now refreshes at rates that were classified a decade ago. Radio-frequency geolocation, synthetic aperture radar, and machine-assisted pattern analysis have turned surface tracking into a subscription service. A warship radiating in the Eastern Mediterranean is a known quantity to anyone willing to pay for the data, and increasingly to anyone willing to scrape it for a fee.

Detection has always been the hard half of the kill chain. Once it becomes cheap, the economics of naval warfare is inverted. A ship that can be found continuously must survive continuously, against munitions that cost a small fraction of its value. That is NATO's real maritime problem, and procurement alone will not solve it. The Alliance cannot out-build its way to advantage at sea, because the thing being contested is no longer mass. It is decision speed.

Each of NATO's maritime theaters is a variation on that single condition, and each demands a different answer.

The High North: The Last Opaque Water

The waters from the Bear Gap to the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap remain the transatlantic hinge. Reinforcements to Europe still move by sea. Whatever the state of Russian industry, the Northern Fleet's submarine force remains the most credible threat to those sea lines.

It is also the one theater where transparency does not yet hold. The undersea domain is still opaque, which is precisely why Russia invests there. Submarines and seabed activity are the remaining sanctuary in an otherwise observable world. Moscow's sustained attention to cables and energy infrastructure, now including the rehearsal near Svalbard, suggests it understands the asymmetry well.

NATO's task in the north is therefore not defensive patrol. It is extending transparency into the last place that lacks it. That means persistent autonomous pickets and fixed and deployable seabed sensors. It means uncrewed underwater vehicles operating on timescales no crewed platform can sustain, and a processing architecture that fuses it all.

Success should be measured by time to detection and time to cue, not by the number of frigates on the plot. Frigates that NATO cannot crew and cannot protect neither improve either condition.

The Baltic: Where Geography Argues Back

The Baltic is different. It is shallow, narrow, and cluttered with islands and commercial traffic, and that environment degrades the sensing advantage transparency depends on. Bottom clutter defeats sonar. Littoral noise defeats classification. Mines remain cheap, legal, deniable, and effective. Whoever occupies the ground beside them can hold or lose the chokepoints that matter.

Sensors do not clear a minefield, and autonomy does not hold an island. Marines, mine countermeasures forces, and special operations teams remain vital in the Baltic in a way they are not in the Norwegian Sea.

The Baltic incidents of recent years, including repeated damage to cables and power interconnectors, were not failures of firepower. They were failures of attribution. The Alliance was too slow to see, too slow to characterize, and too slow to connect a dragged anchor to a named ship.

The Baltic needs a sensing web that knows what happened while it is still happening, and forces postured to contest key terrain when it does. Transparency buys nothing if nothing is ready to act on it.

The Black Sea: The Demonstration Already Happened

Everywhere else, this argument is a forecast. In the Black Sea, it is a finding.

Ukraine, with no meaningful surface fleet, forced Russia to move much of its Black Sea Fleet away from Sevastopol. It did so with shore-based missiles, uncrewed surface vessels, and targeting drawn from allied and commercial sources. Whatever else that campaign proved, it showed that persistent surveillance plus cheap effectors can deny sea control to a navy that normally holds it.

The post-war theater will be shaped by that memory on both sides, and access will remain constrained. The Montreux Convention caps the aggregate tonnage that non-Black Sea powers may keep in the sea and limits their warships' stays to 21 days. Separately, Türkiye has barred belligerent warships from the straits under Article 19 since February 2022, subject to the convention's exception for vessels returning to their home bases. These are distinct levers, and NATO's re-entry planning depends on which one relaxes, and when. Neither is NATO's decision.

The Black Sea will therefore be secured, if it is secured, by its littoral allies. Türkiye, Romania, and Bulgaria will need to operate as a single sensor-shooter architecture. Other allies should contribute data, munitions, uncrewed systems, and shore-based fires rather than visiting hulls. The theater will not become permissive. The realistic objective is to make it transparent and ensure NATO is the party that sees first.

The Mediterranean: Transparent but Crowded

The Mediterranean presents the opposite problem from the High North. It may already be the most transparent sea NATO operates in. It is ringed by allied coastlines, saturated with commercial traffic, and covered by dense sensor networks. Finding ships there is not hard. Making sense of them is.

The strategic picture has also shifted. The fall of the Assad regime has left Russia's naval foothold at Tartus in doubt and its Mediterranean presence diminished. That eases one long-standing challenge without lightening NATO's load. The remaining threats are harder to categorize. They include shadow-fleet tankers of uncertain ownership, activity near undersea cables and pipelines, uncrewed systems in the hands of state and non-state actors, and southern-flank instability that spills into the maritime domain.

In a sea this crowded, the limiting factor is not detection but discrimination. The task is to separate the one vessel that matters from the thousands that do not, fast enough to act. The Mediterranean is where NATO should prove it can turn an overwhelming volume of maritime data into timely decisions. If the Alliance cannot do that in its most observable waters, it will not do it anywhere else.

Measuring the Right Thing

The Svalbard episode is a preview of the maritime contest to come. As satellites, distributed sensors, and AI-enabled analysis make the surface ever more visible, advantage will belong to whoever can see beneath it, make sense of what it sees, and act before the other side does.

That requires NATO to change what it counts. Hulls and tonnage remain necessary, but they are no longer sufficient measures of naval power. The metrics that matter now are time to detect, time to attribute, and time to act, in every theater from the Arctic to the Levant.

An Alliance that measures itself that way will hold the maritime advantage. One that keeps counting ships risks investing in fleets built for a world that no longer exists.

This piece was originally published by Matthew Van Wagenen

item.title: Trump says US will win Iran war 'very soon'
item.description:
By Bo Erickson and Trevor Hunnicutt

item.title: Trump’s Rejection of Iran Offer Highlights Another Big Problem
item.description:
Beijing says artificial intelligence will give the state a visible hand to allocate capital. Here’s the rub: Washington’s economic authority sits in five places, and none of them is in command.

This column begins a four-week series ahead of The Cipher Brief Threat Conference on economic-warfare. The author is hosting a live session on this topic with former Commander of U.S. Special Operations Command, General Bryan Fenton (Ret.). Apply now to attend.

On September 26, the President answered the week's largest security question in just four words: "I'm rejecting their deal." Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, in exchange for lifting the blockade and waiving oil sanctions, had been on the table since September 24. It received its answer in public, from the one official authorized to give it, inside forty-eight hours.

The week's economic questions received no answer of that kind. The trade truce with China, and the pause on Beijing's rare-earth licensing regime tied to it, moved from November 10 to January 10 on the strength of a Treasury Secretary's statement; Beijing has yet to publish a matching notice.

The Russia sanctions act the President signed on September 18 requires determinations on the largest buyers of Russian energy by October 18, a deadline set by Congress rather than the executive, with waivers broad enough to let it pass unenforced. In February, the Supreme Court ruled six to three in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs, removing the instrument the executive had used for its broadest tariffs.

This is important because Washington can decide a war in a sentence. But on the economic front, authority rests with Treasury, Commerce, the U.S. Trade Representative, Congress, and the courts. Each is competent. None is in command. The arrangement is by design and has served the country well for most of the last eighty years. But not anymore.

Beijing is now claiming a different design. In a recent lecture on Xi Jinping's economic strategy, former Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd, who has tracked Chinese ideology for fifty years, described a shift in the Communist Party's theoretical literature. Artificial intelligence (AI) and other "new quality productive forces" are portrayed not only as sources of productivity but also as "a superior macro-allocation mechanism for resources," driven by algorithms. Rudd says the literature now uses the term "the visible hand of the state," offered for the first time as a rival to the market's invisible one. He is careful about its status: the idea sits in the ideological literature, "not yet in the policy literature," and not yet in the behavior of firms. But in his reading, ideology in China is where policy begins.

The hand is already visible without the algorithm. The rare-earth regime now paused until January, the Ministry of Commerce's Announcement No. 61, applies to any product anywhere that carries more than 0.1 percent Chinese-origin rare-earth content by value. One ministry notice imposed it; one more can reimpose it. The capital moves the same way. Chinese households, burned by property and wary of equities, hold record savings in low-yield bank deposits, and the state draws on those deposits through local, provincial, and national loan instruments to fund its technology bet. Rhodium Group puts China's AI capital spending at 932 billion renminbi this year, double last year's, financed by state banks and equity placements rather than bond markets.

America's AI buildout is financed the other way. Its five largest builders raised a net $163 billion in debt in the first half of this year, compared with $90 billion in all of 2025, in a bond market where the ten-year Treasury has reached 5.18 percent, its highest since 2007. No ministry allocated that capital. The market did, and the market will reprice it.

Neither design is simply superior, and the distinction matters more than the verdict. A single allocator is fast and brittle. It can direct capital, licenses, and supply to a strategic target within a week, and it can misallocate at the same speed. The household savings now financing the AI bet were poured into a property boom that left many of those households with assets worth only a fraction of what they paid. A distributed system is slow and resilient. Its errors stay local, its capital carries a price, and no single notice can switch it off. In peacetime competition, resilience compounds. In economic warfare, tempo is the contested variable, and the side that can decide within the other's cycle sets the terms. Beijing has already shown what that looks like. It imposed its rare-earth regime by notice on October 9 of last year and suspended it by another on November 7, having collected in between Washington's agreement to delay its own rule extending export controls to the affiliates of blacklisted firms. Two notices, one month, one American concession.

This column has traced the same gap from the drone fleet to the power grid: the capacity exists, and the decision does not. The economic front shows it at national scale. Washington holds the reserve currency, the deepest capital markets, and the reach of the dollar system. What it lacks is a place to settle competing claims on those instruments and to make them binding on the timeline decided by an adversary.

October 18 is the first live test. The sanctions act's determinations are due that day, just sixteen days before the midterm elections. They will be imposed, waived, or deferred, and whichever it is will say more about the American economic hand than any strategy document published this year. Beijing will be watching the same date, holding a notice it can publish on any morning it chooses.

The question for Washington is who, when economic warfare requires a decision, is empowered to make it, and whether that decision can arrive before the adversary's action. Coordination assigns. Integration arbitrates.

AI Is Coming to the Counter-Drone Fight
item.description:
“Twenty years ago, the state of North Dakota poured in multiple millions of dollars to figure out what it looks like to do beyond visual line-of-sight operations for Class One, Two, and Three Drones. That was just the very nascent stage. Just a decade ago, ten years ago, they figured out that they can do this. They could do this at Grand Forks Air Force Base. Right across from our [air base] runway, on the active duty side, is a place called Grand Sky. It is an innovation research park for all counter-drone operations. It is one of the largest in the United States. They rent the space on our base. It's legitimately federal property that they lease for the research park.”

That was Air Force Col. Alfred J. Rosales, Commander, 319th Reconnaissance Wing, based at Grand Forks Air Force Base, speaking on September 14, at the 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference, as moderator of a panel on Counter-Drone Defense.

I had never heard about what the Grand Forks locals call GrandSKY as a home for Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), where for a decade major defense contractors such as Northrop Grumman and General Atomics have been flight testing and carrying out drone research and development.

Back in May, the Defense Department’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, central authority for the counter-small unmanned aircraft systems program, selected five installations to participate in the directed-energy counter-unmanned aircraft systems pilot program, of which Grand Forks was one.

More recently, as Rosales put it, at the Grand Forks Base, they have been “strapping on vendor equipment” to “build tactics and techniques.” That process will help determine, he said, “How do we want directed-energy weapons to be used inside the United States in FAA [Federal Aviation Agency] controlled airspace, not in the restricted ranges of our Air Force.”

Rosales introduced his September 14, panel whom he said were industry leaders who were “translating technology into trust to allow us to win in the future.”

They were:

Dr. Ben Van Roo, Chief Executive Officer, Legion Intelligence, who, using Artificial Intelligence (AI) was working to get the equipment needed at the tactical level to be able to provide decision-making space without being connected to the Cloud the entire time.

Early on Van Roo said, “We're really still in the infancy right now of how we think about where we're going to use [computer] agents [AI]. What are we going to allow them to decide on? How do they work their way into our TTPs [Tactics, Techniques and Procedures] into our doctrine? And then, the other side, and the big question that we also think about is are they even going to be available?”

Van Roo continued, “The way that we want to use Artificial Intelligence is going to be one, it's still got to be sorted out. What are we going to allow these things [AI] decide to do? Where are they going to work? Into everything from the kill chain to just basic intelligence gathering? And then how are we going to make them more resilient? These are the next layers of challenges that are ahead of us.”

Adam Mohamed, Chief Technology Officer, Asylon Robotics, a Boston Dynamics Partner, who works on autonomous robotics, figuring out how we can layer base defense architecture with our air domain experts.

“Situational awareness is king,” Mohamed said, “because everything else flows from that. And having static situation awareness, mobile situational awareness, being able to understand your battle space is going to take precedence over everything else. The sensor fusion will happen. We'll have the AI. We'll have the ability to operate without a Cloud. But we need to be able to operate when we start losing our sensors, we start losing our radars, we start losing our shooters, and how do we adapt and how does the system adapt for you, because there won't be time for you to make the change to switch over.”

Colton Wood, Chief Technology Officer, Digital Force Technologies, who works on multi-sensor integration. How do we use AI to get the common operating pictures we so desperately desire -- the integration piece that's going to help defeat drones.

Wood said, “Talking about human in the loop is okay. I got a target, I need to go through the process of actually engaging and affecting that target. As we see the threat evolving, that is going to be an incredibly difficult thing to do if I have, you know, multiple threats, multiple targets, multiple different engagement systems…I've set all the rules of engagement. I've set the governance on the systems and then I have a strong decision supported by tools in front of me. But once I've made that decision, I need to be able to engage the systems and machines need to be able to engage the threats, almost autonomously.”

Therefore, Wood explained, “And so I think a lot of simulations, understanding how these systems operate, where the left and right limits are and then allowing these systems to be as effective as they can be without us having to shepherd the process is a very thing that we have to think about [in the] very near future here.”

And finally, Michael Hiatt, Chief Technology Officer, Epirus, who works with Directed-Energy weapons, lasers, the essence of kill-chain dynamics. He comes with skill sets on how to integrate and work in that space.

Hiatt said, “Your risk is very different if you have to literally put metal [kinetic weapons] in the air, you know, with kinetics or, you know, proximate-burst rounds or whatever the kinetic options are. If you can have an option that has lower collateral effects and no collateral damage, you know, which is what the Directed-Energy [DE, laser] weapons offer, you start to be able to change your risk calculation.”


Hiatt continued, “But when for the folks that are on the ground, you know, the battle captain trying to trying to make that assessment, it's not a cost asymmetry problem. It's a magazine depth issue because, you know, what's the reload time on my kinetic? What's the, you know, what's the fly-out time? How many do I, you know, what's my shot doctrine? Do I do a shoot, look, shoot? Do I do a shoot, shoot, look? You know, those are the things that affect magazine consumption.”

Hiatt added, “The reality is you know DE weapons aren't out-ranging kinetic [weapons]. And so when you start to say, ‘All right, I'm going to hold fire on my kinetics. I'm going to let that threat come in closer than I would like because I trust that my DE weapons are going to take it out.’ That's the level of trust that we got to get to.”

At the end of the 41-minute session, Col. Rosales tried to sum it up saying, “This space in counter drones is not a spectator sport. It's for all of us to think through it, industry, academia, the United States Air Force. What I hear is that we are beyond asking what these things are, AI agents, as they incorporate into this picture. We're at the point where we're figuring out what it could look like in terms of policy [so] that we can then get to the next step -- in training and exercising with a rigor to ensure that we have the trust to have our airmen engage when those courses of action are recommended.”

My guess is we are nowhere close to deciding policies where AI fits into the counter-drone fight, nor in warfare itself.

item.title: Clock ticking on Democrat effort to kill flawed US-Saudi nuke deal
item.description:
President Donald Trump may be touting a new nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, but members of Congress are already moving to block it, saying it does not do enough to prevent Saudi Arabia from getting a bomb or impose the same inspection standards required of other nuclear countries.

Democratic Reps. Gregory Meeks, Brad Sherman, John Garamendi, and Don Beyer have introduced a joint resolution of disapproval against the pact, arguing that it lacks two safeguards Washington has sought elsewhere: a commitment against enrichment and reprocessing, and the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol. Their challenge comes amid a war with Iran that has made the region’s nuclear risks even harder to contain than a year ago.

The Democrats’ resolution is important but faces long odds. Democrats would need enough Republican support to pass it in both chambers, and if Trump vetoed it, opponents would need two-thirds majorities in the House and Senate to override him. Furthermore, Congress would have to vote on it during the 90-session-day period of review or the pact takes effect automatically. The clock on that started when Trump sent the deal to Congress in late August.

Irregardless, there are questions swirling around the deal’s viability. First, Trump has made Saudi normalization with Israel a condition. Riyadh continues to insist on a pathway to Palestinian statehood before any normalization with Israel is considered.

Second, the Trump administration’s reluctance to support the Kingdom amidst a wave of attacks by the Houthis is creating tensions. So, while the agreement weakens the standard Washington is seeking in any eventual nuclear negotiation with Tehran, it may fall apart even before its most sensitive nuclear provisions are ever implemented.

What the deal allows and what it leaves out


The agreement submitted to Congress establishes a 30-year framework for peaceful nuclear cooperation. It would allow the United States to transfer nuclear material, equipment, components, and information to Saudi Arabia for peaceful purposes, including technology needed for power reactors. It does not itself deliver a reactor, authorize a particular export, or establish an enrichment facility. Those steps would require further U.S. approvals.

The first red flag has to do with the nuclear fuel cycle. The agreement does not require Riyadh to renounce enrichment or reprocessing, as the United Arab Emirates did in its U.S. nuclear agreement, which is widely considered the “gold standard.”

In his letter to Congress supporting the agreement, Trump explained that the deal “would permit the transfer of material, equipment (including reactors), components, and information for peaceful nuclear purposes” and “the transfer of sensitive nuclear technology to support a joint enrichment and conversion study or upon written agreement of the parties but would not permit the transfer of restricted data.”

In other words, building an enrichment facility and/or reprocessing spent nuclear fuel remain options for Riyadh, which are real proliferation concerns, especially as critics of the deal have pointed out that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman himself has declared both in 2018 and 2023 that “if Iran developed a nuclear bomb, we would follow suit as soon as possible.”

Verification is the other red flag. Saudi Arabia has had a Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement (CSA) with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) since 2009, but a “Small Quantities Protocol” suspended many of its reporting and inspection procedures while the Kingdom had very little nuclear material. Riyadh rescinded that protocol at the end of 2024 as it prepared to expand its civilian nuclear program, bringing the fuller safeguards procedure under the CSA into effect.

The CSA, however, is not part of the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, which gives inspectors broader tools to investigate undeclared activities. The deal does not require the Kingdom to adopt the Additional Protocol either, which is unprecedented. Instead, the agreement calls for additional IAEA verification at sites covered by the U.S.-Saudi cooperation. Congress should therefore ask whether those measures can detect activity outside those sites and what conditions Washington will impose before approving any enrichment cooperation.

Where politics gets in the way


While there are red flags, the nuclear arrangement is less secure politically than its supporters imply. Trump has said adoption depends on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing relations with Israel; the White House said the deal would be off without that step. Saudi leaders continue to advocate for Palestinian statehood as part of any future normalization, and are frustrated with Washington conditioning its nuclear cooperation with the Kingdom on normalization with Israel.

The published nuclear agreement does not explicit state that normalization is a condition. That gap between the president’s public demand and the written nuclear terms could stall implementation before the most difficult technical questions are settled.

The renewed Houthi conflict in Yemen adds another strain. Saudi Arabia has sought stronger U.S. action as Houthi advances threaten its security and Red Sea shipping routes, while Trump has held back from another military escalation. Reporting on the dispute suggests Riyadh and Washington are at odds over what their partnership should require during a regional war.

A strained security bargain gives both sides less room to compromise on conditions relating to the nuclear deal. None of this guarantees the deal’s collapse, but it makes the prospect of a Saudi enrichment project contingent on diplomacy well beyond the nuclear file.

Moreover, even if Congress cannot pass a veto-proof resolution thwarting the current deal, the exercise serves a practical purpose in that hearings and media coverage can press the administration to disclose the safeguards arrangement, explain the status of any side letters, and preserve oversight of export authorizations or enrichment decisions once the pact is cemented.

What policymakers can do


U.S. policymakers should distinguish between helping Saudi Arabia generate nuclear electricity and helping it produce its own nuclear fuel. A power reactor needs fuel, but the country operating it does not have to enrich that fuel. The UAE offers a concrete example: its four Barakah reactors generate electricity using fuel procured through international suppliers, while the UAE has ruled out domestic enrichment.

Saudi Arabia could similarly contract for reactors and buy fabricated fuel assemblies from abroad. Conventional power reactors generally use uranium enriched to about 3-5 percent; they do not require Saudi Arabia to operate centrifuges.

Riyadh might argue that domestic enrichment would protect it against interruptions in foreign supply, which is similar to Tehran’s argument. While that concern deserves an answer, less risky options exist, such as contracts with multiple suppliers, reserves of fabricated fuel, and arrangements for replacement fuel over a reactor’s lifetime.

None of that requires building an enrichment plant in Saudi Arabia. Congress can, therefore, support a civilian power program while setting a separate, much higher bar for any U.S. assistance with enrichment.

The Iran test


The administration’s approach invites a question from nuclear suppliers and nuclear power hopefuls like Tehran: Why is a domestic enrichment option tolerable for Riyadh while enrichment in Iran is treated as an existential danger? One is a friend and the other a stated U.S. foe, but the technology’s proliferation potential is the same either way. Washington also helped strengthen Nuclear Suppliers Group guidance on transfers of enrichment and reprocessing technology. It will be setting a bad example if it starts carving out exceptions for its friends.

A recent Institute of Global Affairs poll found that 43% of Americans believe Iran is more likely to develop a nuclear weapon than it was a year ago, before U.S. attacks on its nuclear facilities. Indeed, having attacked Iran and started a war, the U.S. has no idea how much Tehran is enriching today, if anything. There is no verification.

Congress now has a chance to apply the same test to the Saudi pact: What can inspectors establish, what transfers can still be stopped, and what happens if the political bargain fails? The deal may never reach an enrichment plant. Even so, the rules set during its review will outlast this administration and the current war.

item.title: Venezuela blowback may have a long fuse. They always do.
item.description:
In 1927, Augusto Cesar Sandino began an insurgent campaign against the U.S. occupation of Nicaragua.

Under orders from President Calvin Coolidge, the U.S. Marines had intervened in Nicaragua to settle a civil war between a conservative government and liberal rebels. In his manifesto, Sandino responded by effectively declaring war on the United States. He also specifically denounced former liberal leaders who had agreed to put down their arms in the face of U.S. intervention.

Speaking of General Moncada, the leading liberal officer who had agreed to end his revolt in talks convened by future Secretary of State Henry Stimson, Sandino wrote: “Nobody gave him the authority to abandon the ranks of the revolution to make secret agreements with the enemy.”

One imagines there are Chavistas in Venezuela with similar feelings about interim President Delcy Rodriguez right now.

Having intervened to end the civil war in Nicaragua, the U.S. soon found itself embroiled in a bitter counter-insurgency campaign against Sandino’s men. More than 100 Marines would ultimately be killed in Nicaragua between 1927 and 1933, when the U.S. withdrew and the new Roosevelt administration adopted the Good Neighbor Policy of non-intervention in Latin America’s internal affairs.

Sandino reported no hard feelings, inviting U.S. citizens to come to Nicaragua but “as workers, not as bosses.” Yet Sandino’s happy ending would not last. In 1934, just a year after the U.S. withdrawal, Sandino was captured and executed by Nicaraguan forces loyal to General Anastasio Somoza, who had been trained by the occupying U.S. Marines. In 1936, Somoza took over Nicaragua in a military coup, ruling until his own assassination in 1956. Somoza’s sons would then brutally govern Nicaragua until 1979, when they were overthrown by a new revolutionary group. That group called itself “the Sandinistas” after Augusto Sandino’s rebellion nearly 50 years earlier.

The Sandinistas still rule Nicaragua today. Under the leadership of former revolutionary Daniel Ortega, Nicaragua has become an undemocratic virtual dictatorship. According to Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), Sandinista Nicaragua also poses a national security threat by providing a potential airfield from which Chinese bombers could reach the United States. A similar argument was made back in the 1980s, when the prospect of a communist takeover across Central America motivated the United States to commit or support horrific acts of violence in Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Guatemala.

Fears of a Communist Central America also manifested in popular culture, such as the 1984 film “Red Dawn,” in which Nicaraguan troops join Soviet forces to invade rural Colorado.

Many of these alarms are clearly unfounded, or at least are greatly exaggerated; if China did wish to attack the U.S., they have more effective means of doing so than bombers from Nicaragua. Yet whatever genuine threat Nicaragua does pose should be understood as blowback for the U.S. intervention in Nicaragua all the way back during the Coolidge Administration. Without the U.S. intervention in Nicaragua in 1927, there would have been no Sandino insurgency. Without a Sandino insurgency, then there would have been no Somoza dictatorship, no Sandinista movement, no Contra war, and no Ortega dictatorship today. Possibly no Central American migrant crisis either. What can we learn from this?

Americans are not good at reflecting on history. We tend to judge the failure or success of presidents by two- to four-year election cycles, not the slow burn of resentments and grievances accumulated around the world over decades.

Most Americans, even those who’ve heard of the Iran-Contra Scandal, probably do not know that the U.S. occupied Nicaragua in the late 1920s and the early 1930s. There are likely people working in American politics and government who have heard of the Sandinistas without having heard of Augusto Cesar Sandino, the Sandinista namesake. Could Calvin Coolidge, when he sent the U.S. Marines into Nicaragua in 1927, have possibly imagined he had planted the seeds of considerable trouble for Ronald Reagan in 1987? It’s doubtful.

As the United States heads into the November 2026 midterms, President Donald Trump’s obvious and dramatic foreign policy failures will be on the ballot — first and foremost the disastrous war with Iran. In the face of such a profound failure, the Trump administration is promoting the 2026 capture of Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro as a win. Despite questions about transparency, U.S. officials have eagerly touted a deal to obtain unprecedented control of Venezuela’s oil resources as a direct response to the Iran War-driven energy crisis impacting Americans’ wallets.

Even among critics of the Trump administration’s subsequent Venezuela policy, there seems to be a growing consensus that the military operation to capture Maduro in January was at least a tactical success. Overall, the Donroe Doctrine seems to be working, bringing greater U.S. influence in Latin America than ever. Long gone is the non-interventionist approach of Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s Good Neighbor Policy.

The Trump administration argues the results justify the approach. As Secretary of State Marco Rubio put it: “For the first time in 15, 20 years, the overwhelming majority of the countries in the Western Hemisphere are now led by pro-American leaders and pro-American governments.”

But appearances can be deceiving and success short-lived. Just because a particular foreign policy doesn’t immediately blow up Hormuz-style doesn’t make it wise. Just because the blowback doesn’t arrive before the next election doesn’t mean it never will. Pro-American governments have been brought into being through gunboat diplomacy and open election interference – but for how long?

In all likelihood, there are new Sandinos and new Maduros being created under our noses in places Washington policymakers haven’t heard of — yet. Nearly 8 out of 10 Venezuelans oppose the Trump-Rodriguez deal to let the U.S. take over Venezuela’s oil. Presumably at least some of them will be willing to do something about it. When will their rebellion come? What form will it take? What U.S. response will be best able to mitigate negative consequences while also resolving root causes? Will the U.S. even remember what those root causes are when the day arrives?

These are all questions the Trump administration will not have to face directly. Donald Trump has no more elections to run, and likely won’t live to see the full consequences of the anger he has generated across Latin America.

When the blowback inevitably takes shape, Democrats and Republicans alike should remember that the era of gunboat diplomacy in the early 20th century was followed by an era of revolutions, insurgencies, and even a genuine nuclear crisis in the middle of the 20th century. In the case of Nicaragua, it took nearly 50 years for the bill of 1927-1933 to come due. We’re still paying that tab now.

What will the tab for Trump’s adventurism look like come the second half of the 21st century? Some of us will be unfortunate enough to find out.

item.title: Record number of Dems vote to scrutinize Israeli violence in West Bank
item.description:
Every Senate Democrat but one voted to advance a resolution that would have forced the State Department to produce a report regarding violence against American citizens, as well as other Israeli violations of human rights, in the West Bank. With only Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), however, crossing party lines to support the measure, the resolution failed by a vote of 47-51.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who has consistently been the lone Democratic holdout on a series of Iran war powers votes, once again broke with his party.

Though the resolution ultimately failed, the vote count is nonetheless yet another sign of congressional Democrats’ rapid movement on questions regarding the U.S.-Israel relationship. When Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), one of the co-sponsors of the bill voted on today, introduced similar legislation in January 2024, it failed by a vote of 72-11.

Comparing this result to the vote two and half years ago, John Ramming Chappell, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said it was “remarkable that nearly every Democratic senator voted to scrutinize Israel’s human rights record.”

The resolution was partly a response to nine American citizens who have been killed by Jewish settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank since the start of 2022, and for whom, in the words of Sen. Chris van Hollen (D-Md.), there has been “no accountability” and “no justice.” The Trump administration, notably its ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has occasionally spoken out against the violence but has made no policy changes to address it.

“While the world’s attention has been on Gaza, this same government has been carrying out a slower, but no less brutal campaign in the West Bank. As of last month, the United Nations has documented more than 1400 incidents of settler violence this year alone,” Sanders said on the Senate floor Tuesday.

“The Trump administration, rather than confronting this violence, has lifted sanctions on violent settlers. This violence does not even spare American citizens (...) Enough is enough. The United States cannot continue to bankroll this violence and look the other way,” he added.

The vote was seen as a relatively easy one for Democrats to support, as far as bills critical of Israel are concerned. Had it passed, the legislation would not have automatically led to any policy changes, but rather forced the State Department to produce a report to shed light on human rights abuses. In addition, pro-Israel Democrats have typically been more likely to take votes against Israel when they concern policies in the West Bank as opposed to Gaza.

Speaking to Responsible Statecraft shortly after the bill was introduced in late August, former State Department official Josh Paul, who resigned over the Biden’s administration’s Gaza policy, called rebukes of violent settlers in the West Bank “low-hanging fruit.”

In advance of Tuesday’s vote, Demand Progress senior policy advisor Cavan Kharrazian said in a statement that the resolution was “a long-overdue first step” that “should be the bare minimum for any senator.”

As the party gears up for election seasons where the U.S relationship with Israel is sure to play a central role, Chappell told RS events like these should send a signal.

“This vote is a clear indication for Democratic presidential hopefuls that they will be expected to reevaluate the relationship with an emphasis on accountability and international law,” he said.

item.title: Goodnight Baghdad: US troops leave Iraq after 23 years
item.description:
The Iraq War was already four-years-old when I walked down the ramp of a C-17 at Al Taqaddum Air Base in April 2007. The fact that I am writing these words is proof that I survived that deployment and a subsequent one to Afghanistan in 2013.

In the years since, I transitioned back into civilian life, established a new career, and saw my kids grow up and escape the nest. During nearly all of that time, there were still American troops on the ground in Iraq.

I have a son serving in the military today. He has never been to Iraq, but I can absolutely sympathize with the Iraq veterans who came home from the war only to see their sons or daughters deploy to the same war zone. Because American military service has increasingly become a family affair, there must be a quite a few Thanksgiving conversations where a father listens to his son’s Iraq stories and then retells his own adventure tales that begins with “back in my day in Iraq…”

Had anyone told me while I was dodging IEDs in the summer of 2007 that I would be asked to write a column at the age of 48 about the last American troops leaving Iraq, I would have rightly questioned what the United States was doing there. I believed at the time that we were fighting terrorists and helping to create a free Iraq. Two decades later, I have no idea why we were really fighting there.

I do know that my Marines and I survived some close calls. I also know that nearly 5,000 Americans did not survive their Iraq deployments since the 2003 invasion, along with several hundred thousand other casualties between US contractors, our allies, and the Iraqi people.

A question I wrestle with today is if I had been killed in Iraq, what purpose would my death have served? I don’t have a good answer for that question and the mere fact that the last Americans are coming home from Iraq 19 years later leads me to believe I never will. My grandfather fought in Europe during World War II. He could say that he had helped defeat totalitarianism because his war ended when he was still young. I watched people continuing to deploy to mine after I entered middle age.

At this point, I don’t really want an answer to my question. But I would like to see all that was lost in Iraq: the people who were killed, the broken lives of those who came home, the resources, and even a bit of our collective innocence transform from the waste it is today into a sacrifice. People and societies make sacrifices by relinquishing something of value for some useful purpose. The best way to turn all that was lost in Iraq into a sacrifice is by learning the right lessons from the experience and then properly apply them moving forward.

One such lesson is the limits of military action. The Iraq War began under, to be generous, questionable circumstances and then meandered through a variety of strategies that all shared the same vague goal of a stable, democratic government in Baghdad. Military power wiped out Saddam Hussein's government in a month. Then it took the military supported by all elements of national power more than two decades to get even close to that goal. Baghdad today is less one dictator but still oppressed in so many ways — economically, socially, politically. It is more pro-Iranian and sectarian, with factions that are largely glad to see us go.

Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and now Iran are all cautionary tales. It is hardly a novel observation to note that it is relatively easy to start a war. Ending one is another matter entirely. The United States is pretty good at starting wars. It has a pretty lousy track record at the other end. One of the best things we can do as a society for those we lost in all our recent conflicts is to avoid the messy business of concluding a war by not starting them in the first place.

During stroll through my Arlington neighborhood on Sunday, I walked around the Marine Corps War Memorial. The names and years of all the campaigns in which Marines fought are inscribed around the black granite base of the monument. The inscriptions for Afghanistan and Iraq both have the starting year inscribed, but neither commemoration has an end date. The memorial is currently surrounded by a chain link fence while workers refurbish the iconic statue. It is my earnest hope that this project includes carving the end dates to both of those wars as a tangible sign that they are well and truly over.

It is my earnest prayer that it is a long time before another campaign is added.

The Houthis Took the Red Sea Coast. How Did Washington Miss It?
item.description:
The recent military moves taken by Yemens Houthis resulted in stunning victories and significant strategic gains, virtually unopposed. By taking the Red Sea port of Mocha (Al-Makha), occupying Perim Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and seizing portions of the Red Sea coast, the Iranian proxy group now threatens a key commercial waterway. Reports indicate that, unsurprisingly – or at least it should not be a surprise – Iranian Revolutionary Guard advisors were present, guiding the tactics of Houthi forces. We missed all of this.

For decades, the United States has had an active, robust CIA, diplomatic, and military presence in the Persian Gulf. Understanding, managing, and balancing the nuanced and sometimes fractious relationships among our Gulf allies has always been a complicated task, but one critical to the national security of both the United States and our Gulf allies. We have all made it work, together.

Until now. Something has gone terribly wrong.

As a former CIA operations officer and Chief of Station in the Gulf, I know that failing to anticipate an Iranian-Houthi move of this magnitude is not a tactical error or simply failing to “connect the dots.” Regional actors have their own specific interests and goals in Yemen. Each has taken its turn in the barrel militarily, seemingly largely uncoordinated and sometimes at odds with one another, to discourage or defeat the Houthis. None has succeeded.

What is lacking is leadership, coordination, and overall command and control among the key players: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States. And in the latter’s case, lack of focus.

The current regional conflict seems to have opened rifts in the alliances all of us who served in the Gulf and greater Middle East strove so painstakingly to build and nurture. This is not necessarily through a simple lack of presence or communication; the Commander of CENTCOM was just recently there for consultations, and I have no doubt U.S. military personnel on the ground are in constant and very close contact with their Gulf counterparts. And from my own time there, I am certain U.S. diplomatic and intelligence personnel are equally engaged. This is what we do, and we all do it well.

So how did we miss the Houthi move?

Let’s be clear. This stuff is hard. Anticipating the plans and intentions of an adversary is one of the most important things the intelligence community, and specifically the CIA, does. And the U.S. military has no peer in its planning, logistics, or execution capabilities.

But it is really difficult to anticipate and address the actions of an adversary that relies heavily on asymmetrical warfare.

Particularly when you are dealing with not one but two denied area foes–the U.S. does not have an operational Embassy in either Iran or Yemen. But it can be done; I’ve done it. It just takes focus and, yes, imagination.

But it is important to remember that the intelligence, military, and Diplomatic communities do not operate in a vacuum. Each reports to and receives direction from the White House and DoD. Based on my understanding of how these operate and interact, I can only surmise that the confusion we have seen is emanating from the very top.

Or perhaps an inability, or unwillingness, to manage yet another military crisis.

The U.S.’s lurch into war alongside Israel, one with no apparent end-game, seemingly caught the Gulf Monarchies by surprise. They have suffered the consequences, both militarily and economically. Perhaps ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ - the U.S.’s current intense financial offensive against Iran - will finally bring the Iranian regime to the table to negotiate in good faith. But that remains to be seen. And the Iranians continue to surprise us.

I’ll leave it to others more intimately versed in things Yemeni to analyze the Houthi tactics and strategic goals.

But it should be no surprise that Iran called on the Houthis to make a move at this time. Both the Iranians, and now the Houthis, have proven themselves to be master opportunists. One succeeded in opening a second front in an attempt to lessen the pressure of the U.S. naval blockade and increased sanctions, and the other saw an opportunity to expand their reach. A distracted Washington gave them the opening.

The takeaway: Overconfidence in the ultimate efficacy of Operation Economic Outcast may turn out to be misplaced. If the success of the Houthi advance does not turn out to be an isolated incident, it risks exposing a critical vulnerability in the United States’ strategy. Washington needs to keep its eye on the ball.

item.title: Gen. Burhan digs in as Trump's visa-for-ceasefire scheme blows up
item.description:
On the morning of September 24, Abdel Fattah Burhan should have been standing at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Instead, he was in Khartoum.

The general who leads Sudan’s army and chairs its Sovereignty Council had been offered his American visa on a condition, which, as detailed by Reuters, involved signing the 90-day ceasefire that Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s adviser for Arab and African affairs, had been pitching for months.

Burhan rejected the condition, telling a crowded stadium in Khartoum on September 26 that “we do not want a visa to any country...we will stay here with you until we die here in this country.”

This episode caps a year in which American policy toward Sudan’s civil war has steadily become more hostile toward Burhan and his Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — the very party that Boulos in a May interview called the “constitutional institution” that must be preserved.

Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when its army, the SAF, fell out with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group it once had nurtured. The fighting has produced the world’s largest displacement crisis and famine in parts of the country. Both sides stand accused of atrocities, but the worst have been attributed to the RSF, whose capture of el-Fasher in October 2025 bore what the U.N. called “hallmarks of genocide.”

At present, the SAF holds battlefield momentum. Over the past year, it has clawed back the capital, Khartoum, and swathes of territory in the country's center.

Just days ago, it captured Sodari, a strategic town in North Kordofan state. The string of victories now place the SAF at the gates of Darfur, the RSF’s stronghold and the very region from which the SAF and its allied forces were violently ejected last year when el-Fasher fell.

Given battlefield dynamics and the growing number of high-level defections that are hollowing out the RSF, an outright military victory appears in sight for the first time since the war erupted. It is against this background of shifting momentum that America has ratcheted up pressure, with almost all of it, in practice, on the side that is winning.

Washington has reached for several tools over the last year. In January, 2025, it imposed sanctions on Burhan himself, for refusal “to participate in international peace talks” and “indiscriminate bombing of civilian infrastructure.” Months later, in May 2025, the U.S. government determined that the Government of Sudan, which is led by the SAF, had used chemical weapons.

In early September, a “secret dossier” pointing to chemical weapons use by the SAF was reported by the New York Times and the Washington Post, building on information supplied by a “Middle Eastern intelligence agency.”

The allegation is serious and adds weight to Washington’s earlier determination. However, the program appears to have been wound up, it produced no confirmed fatalities, and the dossier contained no victim testimony.

The dossier originated with Israeli intelligence, according to sources who spoke to Middle East Eye. That detail is significant given Israel’s reported recent contacts with RSF leadership, as well as Israel’s regional alignment that tilts heavily toward the paramilitary group’s primary foreign patron, the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

As the chemical weapons report leaked, the U.S. was also in the process of attempting to expand an arms embargo on Sudan at the U.N. The measure originally restricted weapons flows only to RSF-dominated Darfur; Boulos and America’s U.N. ambassador, Michael Waltz, have pushed to extend it across all of Sudan.

On paper, this is even-handed. It applies to both sides “with no carve-outs,” as Boulos and Waltz explained in a Foreign Policy article. In practice, a blanket embargo hits the army hardest. The SAF is the internationally-recognized government, and its arms purchases are, by that logic, legitimate acts of a state defending itself; an embargo would reclassify those purchases as contraband. The RSF, meanwhile, is a paramilitary with no such standing and therefore has nothing to lose.

Also noteworthy is the fact that Boulos consistently declines to name the UAE. Conflict experts, American lawmakers and America’s own sanctions have identified Abu Dhabi as the RSF’s principal foreign backer, supplying the drones, armored vehicles, and Colombian mercenaries that have given the paramilitary its edge. Asked directly by the BBC about Abu Dhabi’s role, Boulos offered only that “there might be some traders or whatever that are doing these sorts of supplies.”

Indeed, a crucial dynamic shaping Sudan’s civil war is the growing rivalry between the UAE and Saudi Arabia. In November 2025, Crown Prince Muhammad Bin Salman (MBS) pressed President Donald Trump at a White House meeting to get involved in peacemaking in Sudan.

Burhan welcomed the move, and reportedly told MBS by phone before his trip that the war could not end without American pressure on Abu Dhabi. That framework was Riyadh’s, and it was decisively pro-army: Saudi Arabia sees the SAF as a bulwark against state collapse, not as one of two morally equal combatants, as Washington and Abu Dhabi do.

Since Trump’s commitment to “start working on Sudan,” in November, however, the president’s attention has since been consumed by a grinding war with Iran, leaving the Sudan file to Boulos, whose brief spans the entire African continent.

Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, meanwhile, have drifted apart on several fronts. The Emirates quit OPEC, of which Riyadh is the de facto leader, in the spring. It has also deepened defense ties with Israel amid the U.S.-Iran war, while Saudi Arabia has taken an entirely different path, entering into the Mecca Defense Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, a move that is widely viewed as designed to curb Israel’s hawkishness and establish collective deterrence.

Saudi banks have quietly also tightened scrutiny of transfers to the UAE, subjecting them to the kind of enhanced anti-money laundering scrutiny reserved for high-risk jurisdictions. Cargo trucks at the shared border have reportedly been queuing for days this summer awaiting Saudi clearance.

Anwar Gargash, an Emirati presidential adviser, insisted publicly in New York that “the areas of interest between us and Saudi Arabia far outweigh any sort of disagreement.” But the reporting suggests otherwise.

For Riyadh, the stakes in Sudan are only increasing. Its war against the Houthis across its southern border has recently re-opened following Houthi gains along Yemen's western coast. A second fractured state on the Red Sea — one potentially overrun by a group Saudi Arabia neither trusts nor controls — has looked, from Riyadh, like a threat since day one. This fear is what prompted the kingdom to co-host the first round of ceasefire talks in Jeddah at the war’s outset.

As a result, Saudi Arabia is pushing back, and its patience with Washington's handling of the Sudan file appears to be thinning. According to The Africa Report, Riyadh recently threatened to quit the “Quad,” the mediation group convened by Washington, which includes Cairo, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.

In New York, Saudi Arabia's foreign minister sat down with Egypt’s foreign minister, and the foreign ministers of its Mecca Pact partners, Turkey and Pakistan, all of whom back Sudan's army (Turkey supplies drones; Pakistan has sent armoured vehicles). They issued a statement expressing support for Sudan’s “legitimate national institutions" and rejecting “parallel entities” — explicitly pro-army, anti-RSF language from a meeting neither Washington nor Abu Dhabi attended.

Back in Khartoum a few days later, Burhan said Sudan could not be “blackmailed,” in reference to his denied visa. It is not a flattering view of a peace process that needs his cooperation to work. It is also increasingly a view shared by all of America’s Middle Eastern partners, with one exception.

item.title: Escaping the Hormuz trap: What should an agreement to reopen the Strait look like?
item.description:
Escaping the Hormuz trap: What should an agreement to reopen the Strait look like? Expert comment jon.wallace 30 September 2026

A detailed, reciprocal, and verifiable process is essential to ensure that any agreement holds.

The war between the United States and Iran has entered an uncertain phase between escalation and diplomacy. At the UN General Assembly, Iran offered a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks – if various conditions were met. That has apparently been rejected by President Donald Trump.

Subsequent reports claimed the president was considering new strikes on Iran. Meanwhile, attacks on ships from the Iran-backed Houthis have extended the conflict into the Red Sea. 

Given the scope of disagreement between Washington and Tehran, and the global impact of the Strait’s prolonged closure, any settlement will likely need to begin with an unwinding of the Hormuz situation. Can that be achieved?

It is possible. But a successful agreement on Hormuz requires above all a technically precise, reciprocal, and verifiable process that focuses on restoring freedom of navigation. It is unlikely to be effectively addressed through another vague Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), or as part of a wider grand bargain.

Status of the Strait

Tehran has enforced its declared ‘closure’ of the Strait of Hormuz by demanding that ships transit through Iranian waters, charging tolls, and striking vessels it claims have violated its policies. This has resulted in 85 maritime incidents and 24 seafarer deaths reported across the Gulf region.

The US has responded by imposing a blockade on all ships linked to Iran. As of 28 September, US forces have redirected 122 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two. US forces have also created their own route along the southern side of the Strait. The result is an unstable standoff and recurrent clashes. Meanwhile, hundreds of ships remain stranded in the Gulf.

Shipping data shows only 16 vessels crossed the Strait on Monday. That compares to about 138 per day before the start of the war. Most of this traffic along the northern (Iranian) route has been dominated by Iranian, Russian and Chinese-linked vessels. (China purchases over 90 per cent of Iranian exported oil). A large share of US-assisted transits along the southern route are from UAE-flagged vessels.

In August, Iran and Oman moved toward an arrangement for jointly managing maritime traffic in the Strait. Oman’s foreign ministry said the proposed framework would establish a temporary navigational corridor, create a joint project to clear mines, and eventually provide arrangements for information-sharing.

Leaders from Oman, Iran and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) were expected to meet in Muscat to finalize the agreement. But the meeting was postponed in September following US pressure and escalations in the Red Sea. 

The initiative demonstrates that reopening Hormuz does not necessarily require the US and Iran to resolve all their other disputes first. It does, however, require the parties to establish a workable system for commercial navigation. 

For that to happen there will need to be a path toward de-escalation that separates deterrence from punishment. Each side will have to stop trying to inflict excessive ‘punishment’ in response to perceived hostile acts, which merely incentivizes the other to escalate again. 

Make the agreement technically credible

The MOU agreed in June was a first attempt at a diplomatic off-ramp. However, it was riddled with ambiguity. The ceasefire did not hold, and no wider settlement was agreed in the 60-day timeline the MOU set. 

Crucial to the MOU’s failure was the lack of technical detail regarding Hormuz. An effective Strait agreement cannot simply say that traffic of commercial vessels will immediately start. It must define which vessels can transit along which routes and what happens if a vessel deviates from its agreed route. It must state who will provide navigational information and communicate with commercial operators. And it must specify how Iranian, Omani, American, and international maritime authorities will interact.

The MOU anticipated some of these issues. But a durable arrangement will need to create an operating procedure that specifies routes and coordinates, vessel eligibility, communications protocols, rules for navigation and inspection, notification requirements and more.

Most importantly, any agreement must distinguish between commercial and military activity. Commercial vessels need predictable rules as part of a protected commercial-navigation regime – one that does not require the US or Iran to recognize the other’s broader claims beyond Hormuz.

De-escalation must be reciprocal, gradual, and verifiable

The reopening of the Strait should be treated as a process. The Obama administration’s 2015 Iran nuclear deal, much disparaged by President Trump, was a multi-year process. Expert working groups on both sides fed technical agreements into the political process, ensuring the deal was technically achievable as well as politically viable. A process for Hormuz need not be as complex or drawn out. But it will require technical expertise. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Initial efforts at reopening the Strait of Hormuz should focus on stabilizing the maritime environment. Both Iran and the US would need to commit to a progressive and reciprocal pause in hostilities in the Strait. 

For example, Iran could reduce interference with commercial shipping and establish agreed communication procedures. In response, the US and its partners might reduce some blockade operations and provide limited sanctions relief tied to Iran reaching behavioural benchmarks.

Agreement on mine clearance and navigation will also be needed. Technical teams must conduct mine-clearance under a jointly agreed safety protocol, with the locations of cleared and un-cleared areas communicated to commercial operators. 

The parties should establish a common incident-reporting mechanism and require vessels to follow temporary traffic lanes until authorities certify lanes as safe.

Independent maritime organizations could help verify the status of cleared areas without becoming responsible for the political settlement itself.

Repeated, predictable action at sea could build trust between the US, Iran, and other regional actors. The key to success is sequencing and verification. No concession can depend entirely on trust or the kind of broad commitments made in the MOU.

Include multilateral enforcement and monitoring mechanisms

Multilateral engagement could play an important role in creating a lasting deal. Over the course of the conflict, Oman, Qatar and Pakistan have played central mediating roles. And Gulf states have sought arrangements to restore commercial shipping. The UK and France have also organized a multinational coalition to help restore shipping through the Strait. 

Such countries can help implement a reopening by monitoring compliance with an agreement and providing reassurance. The presence of reinforcing powers can also create an ecosystem in which a political agreement is easier for the US and Iran to implement than undermine.

A monitoring mechanism could include representatives from Oman and other Gulf states, international maritime authorities, and neutral technical experts. Its mandate should be narrow and operational. For example, to monitor agreed routes, document incidents and report violations. 

Implementation, not a Grand Bargain

Perhaps the most important element to any agreement is that it allows both sides to describe the outcome as protecting their interests – making each concession conditional on the other side’s behaviour. That makes cooperation less politically risky for both countries.

The way out of the Hormuz trap must therefore be a carefully constructed bargain in which both sides are given a practical, verifiable, and politically survivable way to stop fighting.

The June MOU demonstrated that the basic elements of a US–Iran agreement are conceivable. Its collapse illustrated that political commitments without robust implementation mechanisms and authorities are unlikely to hold. The next agreement must learn from that experience.

Approaching elections in the US and Israel may interfere with progress on reopening the Strait. Some issues, such as Iran’s charging of tolls, could remain a significant political obstacle. But, until the parties establish a durable mechanism for managing traffic in the Strait, the risk of renewed confrontation will remain.
